Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We are moving toward an on-prem + VPC-based deployment for a pilot of Redwood Private and need a short recommendation from you on the transport approach. High-level constraints below: 

- Latency target: steady-state p95 <= 25ms for inference calls from our app tier to the private inference tier (within same region).
- Security/compliance: PCI-scope workloads; log retention for 7 years; strict egress controls (no public-facing endpoints without approval).
- Topology: Two AWS accounts (AppAccount, InferenceAccount) in the same AWS region; the inference layer runs in our on-prem colo behind NAT and a firewall (we have an IPSEC gateway).
- Ops: We cannot open a large set of inbound ports to the inference environment; prefer managed endpoints or few well-known ports.
- Throughput: steady 600 req/s with occasional spikes to 2k req/s; KV-cache reuse desirable.

Attached is a short spreadsheet with current network constraints. Can you outline tradeoffs for VPC Peering vs PrivateLink (interface endpoints) vs site-to-site VPN (IPsec) for this workload, and recommended approach for a pilot + fallbacks? Also include operational impact and any changes to our infra you expect.

Appreciate a concise matrix and next steps — hoping to decide before EOW.

Best,
Sam
Sam Turner
Senior Network Architect — Acme Finance

Thanks Sam — useful constraints, and the sheet was helpful. I attached a short decision matrix (redwood-privatedeploy-transport-matrix.pdf) and flagged the items we need to validate in your environment. High-level thoughts below; Marcus will follow up with a recommended config.

Summary (short):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoint) gives the strongest security posture for cross-account access while minimizing inbound surface area on your inference VPC. It maps well to PCI constraints as traffic never traverses the public internet and we can require mTLS + client certs.
- VPC Peering can offer the lowest raw latency and native IP routing, but it requires broader route and security-team coordination and doesn't support cross-account AWS PrivateLink-like fine-grained service controls. Also peering is regional and can be harder to scale if you want multiple tenants/accounts.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec) is the most flexible for on-prem reachability into a Redwood-managed control plane, but will likely add variability in latency and operational overhead (BGP, NAT traversal, tunnel churn).

Proposed pilot approach: Primary = PrivateLink interface endpoint from AppAccount to our InferenceAccount service (mTLS + flow logs to your SIEM); Fallback = VPC Peering for low-latency batch jobs that require native IP (with strict prefix limits). Use an IPsec S2S only for admin/maintenance channels or where on-prem devices forbid interface endpoints.

Next steps:
1) Marcus — can you draft the config (endpoint ENIs, SGs, route requirements, NAT implications) and an ops runbook?
2) Sam — confirm whether the on-prem firewall team can allow outbound connections to AWS interface endpoints and whether the existing IPsec gateway supports BGP if we need dynamic route failover.
3) Ben — flag any commercial impacts to the pilot configuration (dedicated capacity, SLA) and whether we need a short addendum for PrivateLink provisioning lead times.

Attachment: acme-net-requirements.xlsx (Sam provided) — I included the draft matrix as a separate PDF.

—

Subject: Re: Private deploy transport — detailed tradeoffs and recommended config

On Wed, Jul 13, 2026 at 11:04 AM kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.com> wrote:
> Thanks Sam — useful constraints, and the sheet was helpful. I attached a short decision matrix...

Hi all — dug into the constraints and sketched a practical config. Long but actionable — TL;DR at the top.

TL;DR recommendation: Primary = AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoint) from AppAccount into a service running in your InferenceAccount. PrivateLink + mTLS for session auth, TLS termination in our side with mutual cert verification. Fallback = selective VPC Peering for high-throughput, latency-sensitive paths where PrivateLink latency profile is not meeting SLOs (we can route specific CIDR prefixes). Use S2S IPsec only for management plane and as a last-resort dataplane bridge; do not use IPsec as primary for latency-sensitive inference unless you control both tunnel endpoints and can guarantee stable jitter.

Why PrivateLink first:
- Surface area: AppAccount only needs to create an interface endpoint; no inbound-facing load balancers in your VPC and no long-lived public IPs. This fits PCI requirements and reduces change scope for your firewall team.
- Cross-account access: private DNS override and AWS resource policies allow us to expose a service name to just AppAccount. This gives fine-grained access without broad route table changes.
- TLS/mTLS: We can require client certs per-service and issue short-lived client certs for app nodes; that satisfies mutual-auth expectations for PCI.
- Observability: VPC flow logs + PrivateLink ENI flow captured; Redwood will emit structured logs and can forward to your SIEM via our log-shipping integration.

PrivateLink cons and mitigations:
- Latency: interface endpoints add an extra network hop through the ENI and NLB/MicroLB; expect +2–6ms median in our tests vs peering. For p95-sensitive flows run an early microbenchmark using a dedicated path (we can ship a small load-gen container).
- ENI capacity: if you have many AZs or high concurrency, ensure private endpoint ENIs are provisioned; we'll need to size ENIs and possibly request more endpoint attachments.
- Port limits: interface endpoints map to TCP ports on ENIs; if your app needs arbitrary UDP or non-TCP flows we need peering. Not applicable for standard inference HTTP/gRPC.

Why VPC Peering as fallback:
- Lowest hop-count for same-region IP routing; useful for extremely tight latency budgets.
- Simpler to test with existing networks (no endpoint provisioning), but requires careful routing/security controls (limit accepted prefixes, use prefix lists).

Why IPsec S2S only for management:
- Tunnel jitter and MTU issues: IPsec will vary more in p95 latency and can complicate fragmentation; makes it a risky primary path for production inference traffic.
- NAT/firewall constraints often mean more operational churn.

Operations / runbook highlights:
1) Pilot network test: we (Marcus) will provide a load-generator container and a short scripted test to measure p50/p95 across PrivateLink vs Peering vs IPsec in your environment. Please allow outbound to the interface endpoint IPs and provide an Ops timebox for the test.
2) Routing: AppAccount route table will target the interface endpoint for service FQDN; if peering fallback is enabled we will restrict propagated prefixes to a narrow set (e.g., /28s) to avoid broad route leakage.
3) Security: Require mTLS + client cert rotation (we recommend 24h short-lived certs for app nodes) and enable AWS PrivateLink resource policies to limit callers. Enable strict SGs on the ENIs (only AppAccount app subnets allowed).
4) Observability: Redwood will push structured request metrics and per-request latencies to your SIEM; we recommend exporting VPC flow logs to your Kinesis/SC or S3 for long-term audit.
5) Failover: A health-checking microservice will prefer PrivateLink; on sustained p95 breach (>2 consecutive 5m windows) we can route selective prefixes over a pre-established peering link. Automating this requires BGP or orchestration work — start manual for pilot, automate after we have data.

Sizing/throughput notes tailored to your numbers:
- 600 req/s steady (2k burst): PrivateLink plus NLB-backed service should handle this easily with proper connection pooling and gRPC multiplexing. Ensure our NLB target group has sufficient warm targets in each AZ.
- KV cache reuse: keep requests sticky to the same inference host for cache hits — use consistent hashing at the app side or session affinity at the NLB. PrivateLink does not prevent affinity.

Actionables I will deliver by EOD tomorrow:
- Concrete security group and route table changes (copy/paste).
- A short test plan with seed IPs and a simple bash load-gen.
- A checklist for peering failover (route limits, prefix lists).

If you want me on the call with firewall/WAN folks, I can join Thursday morning (we're flexible).

—
Marcus Lin
Senior SRE, Serving Runtime | Redwood Inference
